protection-vs-security.title: Protection is enforcement inside the system
protection-vs-security.body: Protection mechanisms are the rules the kernel enforces on every access: page permissions, file mode bits, capability checks, and privilege levels. They answer whether a given subject may perform a given operation on a given object. Protection assumes the rules are correct and the identities are genuine. It cannot decide whether a legitimately authorized request is actually wise, and it does nothing about stolen credentials.

protection-vs-security.title: Security adds an adversary to the model
protection-vs-security.body: Security asks what happens when someone deliberately tries to misuse the system. That includes forged identities, malicious inputs, social engineering, physical access, and bugs that let an attacker reach code paths never intended for them. A security design starts from a threat model: which assets matter, who might attack them, which interfaces they can reach, and what the cost of each failure would be.

protection-vs-security.title: Least privilege limits the blast radius
protection-vs-security.body: Even perfect protection cannot stop a component from doing everything it is allowed to do. If a log shipper runs as an administrator, a parsing bug in it becomes an administrator compromise. Giving each component only the identities, files, capabilities, and system calls it needs means that a compromised component can damage only a small, predictable part of the system.

protection-vs-security.title: Defense in depth assumes each layer can fail
protection-vs-security.body: Real systems combine several independent controls: authentication, permission checks, sandboxing, memory protection, auditing, and monitoring. Each layer has gaps, but an attacker must defeat all of them along one path. Operators should be able to explain what stops an attack when one layer fails, and logs should make it possible to discover that a layer was bypassed rather than silently trusting it.

users-groups-and-permissions.title: Real, effective, and saved identities
users-groups-and-permissions.body: A Unix process carries several user and group IDs. The real ID records who started it, the effective ID is used for most permission checks, and the saved ID lets a privileged program drop authority temporarily and regain it later. Set-user-ID executables switch the effective ID on exec, which is why such programs must be small, carefully audited, and avoid trusting their environment.

users-groups-and-permissions.title: How mode bits are evaluated
users-groups-and-permissions.body: For a file, the kernel picks exactly one class: owner if the effective user ID matches, otherwise group if any of the process's groups matches, otherwise other. Only that class's read, write, and execute bits are consulted. A file owner with fewer rights than the group is therefore still restricted. On directories, read lists names, write creates or removes entries, and execute permits traversal and lookup.

users-groups-and-permissions.title: Umask, sticky bits, and ACLs
users-groups-and-permissions.body: New files receive the creating program's requested mode with the process umask bits removed, so a umask of 027 prevents world access by default. The sticky bit on shared directories such as /tmp lets only an entry's owner delete it. POSIX access control lists add named users and groups beyond the three classes, with a mask entry that caps the effective rights of those extra entries.

users-groups-and-permissions.title: Diagnosing a permission denial
users-groups-and-permissions.body: Check the full path, not just the final file, because every directory along the way needs execute permission. Use id to see the process identity and namei -l or ls -ld for each component. Remember that group membership changes only apply to new login sessions, that mandatory access control such as SELinux or AppArmor can deny access the mode bits allow, and that container user remapping changes which host ID really owns files.

access-control-and-capabilities.title: Access control lists versus capability tokens
access-control-and-capabilities.body: An access control list is attached to an object and names who may use it, so the check happens at the object. A capability is an unforgeable token held by the subject that both names an object and grants rights to it. Possessing the token is the permission. Unix file descriptors behave like capabilities: once a file is opened, later reads use the descriptor without re-checking the path's permissions.

access-control-and-capabilities.title: Linux splits root into capabilities
access-control-and-capabilities.body: Traditional root bypassed nearly every check. Linux divides that power into named capabilities such as CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE for low ports, CAP_SYS_ADMIN for many administrative operations, CAP_CHOWN, and CAP_NET_RAW. A process has permitted, effective, inheritable, bounding, and ambient sets that control what it may use now and what survives exec. CAP_SYS_ADMIN is so broad that granting it is close to granting full root.

access-control-and-capabilities.title: Mandatory access control adds system-wide policy
access-control-and-capabilities.body: Discretionary access control lets owners decide who accesses their files. Mandatory access control, implemented in Linux by security modules such as SELinux and AppArmor, applies an administrator-defined policy that owners cannot override. A web server confined by such a policy may be denied reading home directories even when mode bits would allow it, which contains damage from a compromised service.

access-control-and-capabilities.title: The confused deputy problem
access-control-and-capabilities.body: A confused deputy is a privileged program tricked into using its authority for someone else. A compiler service that writes output files with its own permissions could be asked to overwrite a billing log. Capability-style designs avoid this by having the caller pass an already-opened descriptor for the output, so the service only exercises authority the caller actually holds instead of resolving names with its own rights.

memory-protection.title: Page table bits enforce access
memory-protection.body: Each page table entry carries flags such as present, writable, user-accessible, and no-execute. The memory management unit checks them on every access and raises a fault on violation. The kernel then decides whether the fault is legitimate, such as a copy-on-write page or a lazily allocated stack, or an error that becomes a segmentation fault signal delivered to the process.

memory-protection.title: Write xor execute and address randomization
memory-protection.body: Marking writable regions non-executable stops attackers from injecting machine code into a buffer and jumping to it. Attackers responded by reusing existing code fragments, so systems add address space layout randomization, which places the stack, heap, libraries, and executable at unpredictable addresses each run. An attacker who cannot predict addresses cannot easily chain reusable code without first leaking a pointer.

memory-protection.title: Guard pages, canaries, and hardened allocators
memory-protection.body: An unmapped guard page below each thread stack turns a stack overflow into an immediate fault instead of silent corruption of neighboring memory. Compilers insert stack canaries, values checked before a function returns, to detect overwritten return addresses. Hardened allocators separate metadata from user data and randomize placement so heap overflows are harder to turn into reliable control over the program.

memory-protection.title: Kernel-side protections
memory-protection.body: The kernel protects itself too. Supervisor mode access prevention and execution prevention stop the kernel from accidentally reading or running user-space memory, which blocks a class of exploits that plant data in user pages. Kernel address randomization, read-only data after initialization, and page table isolation between user and kernel mappings each remove a step that attackers previously relied upon.

seccomp-and-syscall-filtering.title: How a seccomp filter evaluates a call
seccomp-and-syscall-filtering.body: Seccomp in filter mode attaches a small classic BPF program to a thread. On every system call the kernel runs it with the call number, architecture, and argument values. The program returns an action: allow, return an error code, send a signal, kill the thread or process, or notify a supervisor. Filters are inherited across fork and exec and can only be made stricter, never removed.

seccomp-and-syscall-filtering.title: Allow-lists beat deny-lists
seccomp-and-syscall-filtering.body: A deny-list blocks known dangerous calls but silently permits any new or forgotten one. An allow-list names exactly the calls the program needs and rejects everything else, so the exposed kernel surface shrinks to what was reviewed. The filter must also check the architecture field, because the same number means different calls on 32-bit and 64-bit interfaces.

seccomp-and-syscall-filtering.title: Argument checks and their limits
seccomp-and-syscall-filtering.body: Filters can inspect integer arguments, for example allowing socket only for a particular address family or ioctl only with specific request codes. They cannot safely inspect pointer arguments such as path strings, because user memory could change between the check and the kernel's use. Path-based restrictions therefore belong in mechanisms like Landlock or mandatory access control rather than in seccomp.

seccomp-and-syscall-filtering.title: Building and testing a profile
seccomp-and-syscall-filtering.body: Profiles usually start by tracing a representative workload with strace or audit logging to collect required calls, then running in a logging mode before enforcing. Container runtimes apply a default profile that blocks rarely needed calls such as kernel module loading. Library or runtime upgrades can introduce new calls, so profiles need regression tests and failures should be visible rather than surfacing as confusing permission errors.

resource-limits.title: Soft and hard rlimits
resource-limits.body: Each process has per-resource limits with a soft value that is enforced and a hard ceiling. An unprivileged process may raise its soft limit up to the hard limit, or lower the hard limit, but cannot raise the hard limit. Common limits include open files, processes per user, address space, core file size, and CPU seconds. Limits are inherited by children and can be inspected in /proc/PID/limits.

resource-limits.title: What happens when a limit is hit
resource-limits.body: Limits fail in specific ways. Exceeding the open file limit makes open, accept, and socket return EMFILE. Exceeding the process limit makes fork return EAGAIN. Going past the CPU time soft limit delivers SIGXCPU and the hard limit kills the process. Programs that ignore these errors often spin in retry loops or crash far from the real cause, so the specific error code is the key clue.

resource-limits.title: Per-process limits versus group limits
resource-limits.body: Rlimits apply to individual processes or users, so a service that forks many workers can still consume a whole machine. Control groups account for a set of processes together, capping total memory, CPU share, process count, and IO for the whole service. Production systems usually combine both: rlimits to catch runaway single processes and cgroups to bound the service as a unit.

resource-limits.title: Choosing values deliberately
resource-limits.body: Limits that are too low cause outages under legitimate load, while limits that are too high do not protect anything. Base them on measured peak usage plus headroom, document why each value exists, and set them where the service is defined, such as the systemd unit or container specification, instead of relying on whatever a login shell happened to inherit.

common-os-vulnerabilities.title: Memory safety errors
common-os-vulnerabilities.body: Buffer overflows, use-after-free, double free, and integer overflow in size calculations remain the largest source of serious vulnerabilities in kernels and system software written in C and C++. They let attackers corrupt adjacent data or control flow. Mitigations make exploitation harder, but the durable fix is bounds-checked code, careful arithmetic on sizes, fuzzing, and increasingly memory-safe languages for new components.

common-os-vulnerabilities.title: Time-of-check to time-of-use races
common-os-vulnerabilities.body: A privileged program that checks a path with access and then opens it gives an attacker a window to replace the file with a symbolic link to something sensitive. The check and the use refer to different objects. Safer code opens first and then inspects the descriptor with fstat, uses openat with flags that refuse symbolic links, and avoids predictable names in shared directories like /tmp.

common-os-vulnerabilities.title: Privilege escalation paths
common-os-vulnerabilities.body: Escalation happens when a lower-privileged actor reaches higher authority: a vulnerable set-user-ID binary, a writable script executed by root's scheduled job, a world-writable directory early in a privileged PATH, an exposed container runtime socket, or a kernel bug reachable through an unusual system call. Auditing for these paths means following what privileged code executes, reads, and trusts.

common-os-vulnerabilities.title: Patching and exposure management
common-os-vulnerabilities.body: Most real compromises use known vulnerabilities that already had fixes. Keeping kernels and packages updated, tracking which hosts run which versions, and rebooting or live-patching to actually load the fixed kernel matter as much as clever defenses. Reducing exposed surface, such as disabling unused services, kernel modules, and network listeners, shrinks the number of vulnerabilities that can matter at all.

side-channels.title: Timing reveals data-dependent work
side-channels.body: If a computation takes different amounts of time depending on a secret, an observer measuring many runs can infer the secret. Early-exit comparisons, table lookups indexed by key bytes, and branching on secret bits all leak this way. Cryptographic code uses constant-time techniques so execution time and memory access patterns are independent of secret values.

side-channels.title: Caches as a shared measuring device
side-channels.body: Processes on the same core or socket share caches. An attacker can fill a cache set, let the victim run, and time its own accesses to learn which lines the victim touched, or flush shared library lines and see which ones came back. These prime-and-probe and flush-and-reload techniques turn ordinary performance behavior into an information channel across protection boundaries.

side-channels.title: Speculative execution attacks
side-channels.body: Modern processors execute instructions speculatively before knowing whether they should run. Results are discarded when the guess is wrong, but cache side effects remain. Attacks in the Spectre and Meltdown families steer speculation to read data across boundaries and then recover it through cache timing. Mitigations include kernel page table isolation, retpolines, speculation barriers, and microcode updates, often with measurable performance cost.

side-channels.title: Mitigation as a policy decision
side-channels.body: Some mitigations disable simultaneous multithreading, flush buffers on context switches, or isolate tenants onto separate cores. These choices trade throughput for isolation. A single-tenant batch cluster may accept different settings than a multi-tenant cloud host. Operators should know which mitigations their kernel enables, which are reported in /sys/devices/system/cpu/vulnerabilities, and why.

what-virtualization-is.title: Virtualization is an illusion managed by software
what-virtualization-is.body: Virtualization gives a consumer an interface that looks like a dedicated resource while software maps it onto shared physical resources. Virtual memory gives each process a private address space, a hypervisor gives each guest what looks like a whole computer, and a container gives a process group its own view of files and process IDs. The consumer programs against the illusion; the manager enforces sharing.

what-virtualization-is.title: Popek and Goldberg requirements
what-virtualization-is.body: A classic definition says a virtual machine monitor must provide equivalence, so programs behave as on real hardware; resource control, so the monitor stays in charge; and efficiency, so most instructions run directly. Older x86 processors had sensitive instructions that did not trap, which broke these rules until binary translation and later hardware extensions made efficient trap-and-emulate virtualization possible.

what-virtualization-is.title: Hardware support changed the design
what-virtualization-is.body: Intel VT-x and AMD-V add a guest execution mode where sensitive operations cause controlled exits to the hypervisor. Nested page tables let hardware walk guest and host mappings together, and IOMMUs let devices be assigned safely to guests. These features moved much of the work from software tricks into the processor, which is why modern virtual machines run most code at near-native speed.

what-virtualization-is.title: Overcommitment and its consequences
what-virtualization-is.body: Because guests rarely use everything at once, providers allocate more virtual CPUs and memory than the host physically has. This raises utilization, but when guests peak together they compete. A guest may see steal time, where its virtual CPU was ready but the host ran something else, or memory reclaimed through ballooning. Performance analysis inside a guest must account for this hidden contention.

virtual-machines-and-hypervisors.title: Type 1 and Type 2 hypervisors
virtual-machines-and-hypervisors.body: A Type 1 hypervisor runs directly on hardware and hosts guests, as in Xen or VMware ESXi. A Type 2 hypervisor runs as an application on a host operating system, as with desktop virtualization tools. KVM blurs the categories: it turns the Linux kernel itself into a hypervisor, with each guest running as a normal process that the host scheduler manages.

virtual-machines-and-hypervisors.title: VM exits are the main overhead
virtual-machines-and-hypervisors.body: Most guest instructions run natively. Control returns to the hypervisor on a VM exit, triggered by privileged operations, certain interrupts, port or memory-mapped IO to emulated devices, and some page faults. Each exit costs time saving and restoring state. Workloads that perform frequent IO through emulated devices suffer most, which is why exit counts are a key metric when tuning virtual machines.

virtual-machines-and-hypervisors.title: Device virtualization options
virtual-machines-and-hypervisors.body: Fully emulated devices mimic real hardware and work with unmodified drivers but are slow. Paravirtualized devices such as virtio use a simple shared-memory ring designed for virtualization, so guests batch requests with few exits. Device passthrough and SR-IOV give a guest direct access to hardware through the IOMMU, offering near-native performance at the cost of easy live migration.

virtual-machines-and-hypervisors.title: Snapshots and live migration
virtual-machines-and-hypervisors.body: Because a virtual machine's state is data, it can be saved, cloned, or moved. Live migration copies memory to another host while the guest runs, repeatedly sending pages that were modified, then briefly pauses to transfer the remainder and CPU state. Write-heavy guests take longer to converge, and operators must ensure storage and networks are reachable from the destination.

virtualized-memory.title: Guest physical is not host physical
virtualized-memory.body: A guest kernel manages what it believes is physical memory, but those addresses are themselves virtual from the host's point of view. A guest virtual address goes through the guest page tables to a guest physical address, and then through the hypervisor's mapping to a host physical address. Both translations must succeed for an access to complete.

virtualized-memory.title: Shadow and nested page tables
virtualized-memory.body: Before hardware support, hypervisors maintained shadow page tables that combined both translations, intercepting every guest page table change. Nested or extended page tables let the MMU walk both levels itself. This removes most interception but makes a TLB miss expensive, potentially requiring many memory references, so huge pages on both guest and host noticeably improve memory-heavy virtualized workloads.

virtualized-memory.title: Reclaiming memory from guests
virtualized-memory.body: Hosts recover memory through several techniques. A balloon driver inside the guest allocates pages and returns them to the hypervisor, letting the guest decide what to give up. Kernel same-page merging deduplicates identical pages across guests with copy-on-write. As a last resort the host can swap guest memory, which is slow because the guest does not know which pages are cold.

virtualized-memory.title: Diagnosing memory pressure in a guest
virtualized-memory.body: A guest may look healthy by its own metrics while the host is swapping it, producing unexplained latency. Look for balloon size changes, steal time, and major page faults that do not match the guest's own swap activity. Reserving memory for latency-sensitive guests and avoiding aggressive overcommitment is often more reliable than tuning inside the guest.

containers-vs-virtual-machines.title: One kernel versus many
containers-vs-virtual-machines.body: Containers are ordinary processes on the host kernel, isolated with namespaces, limited with cgroups, and given a separate root file system. Virtual machines run their own kernels on virtual hardware. Containers therefore start in milliseconds and share memory efficiently, while virtual machines can run different kernels and operating systems and present a much smaller interface between tenant and host.

containers-vs-virtual-machines.title: Isolation strength and attack surface
containers-vs-virtual-machines.body: A container escape requires a bug in the shared kernel or a misconfiguration, and the full system call interface is reachable from inside. A virtual machine escape requires a bug in the hypervisor or its device emulation, a smaller and more constrained surface. For mutually untrusted tenants, providers commonly place containers inside lightweight virtual machines to combine both models.

containers-vs-virtual-machines.title: Sandboxed runtimes in between
containers-vs-virtual-machines.body: Projects such as gVisor intercept a container's system calls in a user-space kernel, and microVM runtimes such as Firecracker or Kata Containers boot a minimal virtual machine per container or pod. They keep the container packaging and workflow while adding a stronger boundary, at some cost in startup time, compatibility, and system call performance.

containers-vs-virtual-machines.title: Choosing between them
containers-vs-virtual-machines.body: Pick containers for dense packing of trusted services built for the same kernel and for fast scaling. Pick virtual machines when you need a different kernel, strong tenant isolation, kernel modules, or hardware-level guarantees. Many platforms use both: virtual machines as the security and capacity unit, and containers inside them as the deployment unit.

namespaces.title: The namespace types
namespaces.body: Linux provides separate namespaces for mount points, process IDs, network stacks, hostnames, System V IPC, user and group IDs, control group views, and time offsets. Each process belongs to exactly one namespace of each type. Creating a new namespace gives the process a private copy of that view, while everything else remains shared with the processes around it.

namespaces.title: Creating and joining namespaces
namespaces.body: The clone system call with CLONE_NEW flags starts a child in new namespaces, unshare moves the caller into new ones, and setns joins an existing namespace through a file descriptor from /proc/PID/ns. Tools such as unshare, nsenter, and ip netns wrap these calls. Container runtimes combine them to build the environment before executing the application.

namespaces.title: User namespaces enable rootless containers
namespaces.body: A user namespace maps a range of host user IDs to IDs inside the namespace, so a process can be root inside while being an ordinary user outside. Capabilities held inside apply only to resources owned by that namespace. This lets unprivileged users build containers safely, though it also exposes more kernel code to unprivileged users, which some distributions restrict.

namespaces.title: What namespaces do not isolate
namespaces.body: Namespaces change what a process can name and see, not how much it can consume. They do not limit CPU, memory, or IO; that is the job of cgroups. Kernel-global resources like the system clock, many sysctl settings, kernel keyrings, and the kernel itself remain shared. A namespace boundary is a view boundary, and security depends on combining it with other controls.

cgroups.title: The cgroup v2 hierarchy
cgroups.body: Control groups organize processes into a tree mounted as a file system, typically at /sys/fs/cgroup. Each directory is a group with interface files for enabled controllers. In version 2 there is one unified hierarchy, processes live only in leaf groups, and controllers are enabled per subtree. Systemd creates slices and scopes so that every service and session has its own group.

cgroups.title: CPU control: weights and quotas
cgroups.body: The cpu.weight file sets a proportional share used only under contention, while cpu.max sets a hard quota such as 50 milliseconds per 100 millisecond period. Quotas cause throttling even when the host is idle, which surprises applications that sized thread pools by visible core count. The cpu.stat file reports nr_throttled and throttled_usec, the first place to look for unexplained latency.

cgroups.title: Memory control and the OOM killer
cgroups.body: The memory.max file sets a hard limit, memory.high triggers reclaim and throttling before the hard limit, and memory.low protects a group's memory from reclaim. Page cache counts toward usage, so file-heavy workloads can approach limits without large heaps. When reclaim fails at memory.max, the kernel runs the OOM killer within that group, and memory.events records the oom_kill counter.

cgroups.title: IO, process counts, and pressure stall information
cgroups.body: The io.max and io.weight files throttle and prioritize block device bandwidth and operations, and pids.max caps how many tasks a group may create, stopping fork bombs. Each group also exposes pressure stall information in cpu.pressure, memory.pressure, and io.pressure, showing the share of time tasks were delayed waiting for that resource, which is more direct than raw utilization.

container-file-systems.title: Image layers and union mounts
container-file-systems.body: A container image is a stack of read-only layers, each recording files added, changed, or deleted relative to the previous one. At run time a union file system such as overlayfs presents the layers merged into one tree and adds a thin writable layer on top. Many containers can share the same lower layers on disk and in page cache.

container-file-systems.title: Copy-up and whiteouts
container-file-systems.body: When a container first modifies a file from a lower layer, overlayfs copies the whole file into the writable layer, then applies the change. Deleting a lower-layer file creates a whiteout marker that hides it. Large files modified slightly, such as databases in an image, therefore cost a full copy and should live on volumes instead of the container's own file system.

container-file-systems.title: Volumes and bind mounts
container-file-systems.body: Data that must outlive a container belongs in a volume or bind mount, which bypasses the union file system and maps a host or network directory into the container. These mounts keep the host's ownership and permissions, so user ID mismatches between image and host are a common cause of permission errors when a container writes to a mounted directory.

container-file-systems.title: Keeping images small and reproducible
container-file-systems.body: Every instruction that changes files usually creates a layer, and deleting files in a later layer does not shrink earlier ones. Multi-stage builds copy only the final artifacts into a minimal runtime image. Smaller images pull faster, start faster, and contain fewer packages that can carry vulnerabilities, and pinning base image digests makes builds repeatable.

pid-1-and-signal-handling.title: PID 1 ignores default signal actions
pid-1-and-signal-handling.body: The kernel treats the first process in a PID namespace specially: signals with default actions, such as SIGTERM, are not delivered unless the process installed a handler. An application that relies on the default action to exit will ignore a stop request when it runs as PID 1. The runtime then waits for its timeout and kills the container with SIGKILL, skipping graceful shutdown.

pid-1-and-signal-handling.title: Reaping orphaned children
pid-1-and-signal-handling.body: When a process exits, its parent must call wait to collect the exit status, otherwise the entry remains as a zombie. Orphaned processes are reparented to PID 1 of their namespace. An application that spawns helpers or shell commands but never reaps unknown children slowly accumulates zombies, which eventually exhaust the process ID limit of the container.

pid-1-and-signal-handling.title: Shell wrappers swallow signals
pid-1-and-signal-handling.body: Starting a container with a shell form command makes the shell PID 1 and the application its child. Many shells do not forward SIGTERM to children, so the application never hears about shutdown. Using the exec form of the entrypoint, or ending wrapper scripts with exec so the application replaces the shell, keeps the application directly receiving signals.

pid-1-and-signal-handling.title: Minimal init processes
pid-1-and-signal-handling.body: Small init programs such as tini or dumb-init run as PID 1, forward signals to the application, and reap zombies. Many runtimes can inject one with an option. The application should still handle SIGTERM by stopping new work, finishing in-flight requests, flushing data, and exiting before the orchestrator's grace period ends.

container-resource-failures.title: Applications that size themselves from the host
container-resource-failures.body: Software often reads total memory and processor count to size heaps, caches, and thread pools. Inside a container those host values can be far larger than the cgroup allows. Runtimes that are not container-aware may set a heap bigger than the memory limit or spawn dozens of threads competing for a small CPU quota. Modern runtimes read cgroup limits, but configuration should still be explicit.

container-resource-failures.title: OOM kills look like silent restarts
container-resource-failures.body: When a container exceeds its memory limit the kernel kills a process inside it with SIGKILL, so there is no stack trace or application log. The orchestrator reports an OOMKilled reason and exit code 137. The usual causes are heap plus native memory, thread stacks, and page cache exceeding the limit together, not just the configured heap size.

container-resource-failures.title: CPU throttling shows up as tail latency
container-resource-failures.body: A container with a CPU quota can be throttled for the remainder of each period after bursting, even when average usage is low. Requests arriving during throttled intervals wait, inflating p99 latency while dashboards show modest utilization. Checking throttled time, reducing parallelism to fit the quota, or relaxing hard limits in favor of weights usually resolves it.

container-resource-failures.title: Disk and descriptor limits inside containers
container-resource-failures.body: Writable layers and ephemeral storage can fill up from logs or temporary files, causing write failures or eviction by the orchestrator. Process and file descriptor limits apply too, so a leak that a large host would tolerate fails quickly in a container. Monitoring each limit separately, with the specific error it produces, makes these failures diagnosable instead of mysterious.

container-security.title: Root in a container is still powerful
container-security.body: Without user namespaces, root inside a container is the same user ID as root on the host, limited only by dropped capabilities, seccomp, and mandatory access control. A kernel bug or a mounted host path can turn that into host root. Running as a non-root user, using rootless runtimes, and setting the no-new-privileges flag remove much of this risk.

container-security.title: Dangerous configurations
container-security.body: Privileged mode disables most isolation. Mounting the container runtime socket gives control over every container on the host. Host network or host PID namespaces expose host services and processes. Writable mounts of sensitive host directories allow persistence. Each of these is sometimes requested for convenience, and each should be treated as granting host-level access.

container-security.title: Supply chain and image hygiene
container-security.body: An image runs whatever its layers contain. Use trusted base images, rebuild regularly to pick up patches, scan for known vulnerabilities, and avoid putting secrets in layers where anyone with the image can read them. Signing images and verifying signatures at deployment prevents running an image that was altered after it was built.

container-security.title: Runtime monitoring and least privilege
container-security.body: Drop all capabilities and add back only what is required, keep the root file system read-only with explicit writable volumes, and apply seccomp and AppArmor or SELinux profiles. Runtime monitoring can flag unexpected behavior such as shells spawning in production containers or writes to system directories, catching compromises that preventive controls missed.

a-systematic-debugging-method.title: Define the problem precisely
a-systematic-debugging-method.body: Start by stating what is wrong in measurable terms: which requests, which hosts, since when, how much slower or how often failing, compared with what baseline. Vague reports such as the system is slow lead to random exploration. Ask what changed recently, including deployments, configuration, traffic, and dependencies, because most incidents follow a change.

a-systematic-debugging-method.title: Use resource checklists such as USE
a-systematic-debugging-method.body: The USE method checks every resource for utilization, saturation, and errors: CPUs, memory, disks, network interfaces, and software resources like locks and connection pools. Saturation, meaning queued work, usually explains latency better than utilization. Working through a fixed checklist prevents tunnel vision on the first plausible cause and quickly rules out healthy components.

a-systematic-debugging-method.title: Narrow with experiments, not assumptions
a-systematic-debugging-method.body: Form a hypothesis that predicts something observable, then test it with the cheapest measurement that could prove it wrong. Bisect deployments or configuration when a change is suspected. Reproduce the problem in isolation when possible. Change one thing at a time and record what was observed, so later steps do not rest on conclusions nobody actually verified.

a-systematic-debugging-method.title: Close the loop
a-systematic-debugging-method.body: A fix is only confirmed when the original symptom metric returns to baseline and stays there. Afterwards, write down the cause, the evidence, and what would have detected it earlier. Adding the missing metric, alert, or test turns one investigation into lasting protection and builds the shared knowledge that speeds up the next incident.

investigating-processes.title: Reading ps and process states
investigating-processes.body: The ps command shows each process's state: R running or runnable, S interruptible sleep, D uninterruptible sleep usually waiting on IO, T stopped, and Z zombie. Many tasks in D state point at storage or network file systems. Useful columns include parent PID, start time, CPU time, resident memory, and the full command line, which distinguishes similar workers.

investigating-processes.title: The /proc file system
investigating-processes.body: Each process has a directory under /proc containing its command line, environment, current working directory, open descriptors in fd, memory maps in maps and smaps, resource limits, cgroup membership, namespaces, and scheduling statistics. These files are what tools like ps and top read, and inspecting them directly answers questions the tools do not show.

investigating-processes.title: Process trees and supervisors
investigating-processes.body: Viewing the hierarchy with pstree or ps with forest output reveals which supervisor started a process and how workers relate to a master. Restarting the right unit through its supervisor, such as a systemd service, is safer than killing individual PIDs, which may simply be replaced. Logs from the supervisor also record exits, signals, and restart loops.

investigating-processes.title: Thread-level views
investigating-processes.body: A process can contain many threads with different behavior. Use top with thread mode or ps with thread options to see per-thread CPU, and match thread IDs to names set by the application. A single hot thread in an otherwise idle process often indicates a busy loop, a lock holder, or an event loop doing blocking work.

investigating-cpu.title: Load average is not CPU usage
investigating-cpu.body: On Linux the load average counts tasks that are runnable plus those in uninterruptible sleep, averaged over one, five, and fifteen minutes. A high load with idle CPUs often means tasks are blocked on IO. Compare load with the number of cores and with actual CPU utilization before concluding that the processors are overloaded.

investigating-cpu.title: Breaking down CPU time
investigating-cpu.body: Tools such as mpstat and top split time into user, system, IO wait, interrupt handling, and steal. High system time suggests heavy system call or kernel activity, high steal means a hypervisor is running other guests, and uneven usage across cores reveals single-threaded bottlenecks or interrupts pinned to one CPU. Averages across all cores can hide a single saturated one.

investigating-cpu.title: Run queue latency and context switches
investigating-cpu.body: Scheduler delay, the time a task waits runnable before getting a CPU, directly adds to request latency. It can be measured from /proc scheduling statistics, perf sched, or BPF tools. Very high voluntary context switch counts suggest frequent blocking, while involuntary switches indicate contention for CPUs. Throttling in cgroups produces similar delays without high host utilization.

investigating-cpu.title: Finding where cycles go
investigating-cpu.body: Once CPU is confirmed as the bottleneck, sample stacks with perf or a language profiler to find hot functions. Hardware counters show instructions per cycle, cache misses, and branch mispredictions, distinguishing code that executes too much from code that stalls on memory. Optimizing without a profile frequently targets code that is not actually on the hot path.

investigating-memory.title: Reading free and meminfo correctly
investigating-memory.body: Free memory near zero is normal because Linux uses spare memory for page cache. The available figure estimates how much can be allocated without swapping, and is the number to watch. /proc/meminfo breaks usage into anonymous memory, cache, slab, shared memory, and more, helping identify whether growth belongs to applications, file cache, or kernel structures.

investigating-memory.title: Per-process memory metrics
investigating-memory.body: Virtual size counts everything mapped, including reserved but untouched regions, so it is rarely meaningful. Resident set size counts pages currently in RAM but double counts shared libraries. Proportional set size divides shared pages among users, and unique set size counts only private pages. smaps_rollup in /proc reports these figures, and private dirty memory is often the best leak indicator.

investigating-memory.title: Paging, swapping, and the OOM killer
investigating-memory.body: Major page faults that read from disk, rising swap activity in vmstat, and memory pressure stall information indicate genuine memory shortage. When reclaim cannot free enough, the OOM killer chooses a victim by a badness score adjustable with oom_score_adj. Kernel logs record each kill with the memory state at that moment, which explains sudden process disappearances.

investigating-memory.title: Native versus managed leaks
investigating-memory.body: In garbage-collected languages, a heap dump shows which objects are retained and by what references. Growth outside the managed heap, from native libraries, thread stacks, memory-mapped files, or allocator fragmentation, needs different tools such as allocator statistics, BPF-based allocation tracing, or comparing smaps over time to find which mappings grow.

investigating-disk.title: Latency, throughput, and queue depth
investigating-disk.body: The iostat extended view reports per-device reads and writes per second, throughput, average request size, average wait time, and queue size. Utilization near 100 percent means a single-queue device is always busy, but modern SSDs and NVMe devices serve many requests in parallel, so latency and queue depth are better saturation signals than utilization alone.

investigating-disk.title: Which process causes the IO
investigating-disk.body: Tools such as iotop and pidstat with IO reporting attribute reads and writes to processes. BPF tools like biolatency and biosnoop show latency histograms and individual requests with the issuing process. Writes are often issued later by kernel writeback threads rather than the application, so dirty page statistics and fsync calls are needed to connect cause and effect.

investigating-disk.title: Capacity versus inodes and reservations
investigating-disk.body: A file system can refuse new files when it runs out of inodes even with free space, which df -i reveals. Deleted files still held open by a process keep consuming space until closed, visible through lsof listing deleted entries. Some file systems reserve blocks for root, so ordinary users see the disk as full slightly earlier than root does.

investigating-disk.title: Cache effects on measurements
investigating-disk.body: Reads served from page cache never reach the device, so benchmarks and production behavior differ depending on what is cached. A process that suddenly becomes disk-bound after memory pressure evicted its working set shows rising read latency and major faults together. Checking cache hit behavior prevents blaming the disk for what is really a memory problem.

investigating-system-calls.title: Using strace effectively
investigating-system-calls.body: strace prints each system call with arguments, return values, and errors. Following children with -f, timestamping with -tt, and showing time spent in each call with -T reveal slow or failing operations. The summary mode with -c counts calls and errors. Filtering by class, such as file or network calls, keeps output readable on busy processes.

investigating-system-calls.title: Overhead and safer alternatives
investigating-system-calls.body: Traditional strace uses ptrace, which stops the traced process on every system call and can slow it dramatically, so attaching to a busy production service is risky. perf trace and BPF-based tools observe system calls with much lower overhead, aggregating in the kernel. Choose the lighter tool first on production systems and use strace for detailed reproduction.

investigating-system-calls.title: Interpreting error codes
investigating-system-calls.body: Errors are clues, not necessarily the bug. ENOENT during startup may be a normal search through configuration paths. EAGAIN on non-blocking sockets is expected. EMFILE, ENOSPC, EACCES, and ETIMEDOUT usually point at real resource or permission problems. Look for the call whose failure the application actually acted on, typically the last error before visible misbehavior.

investigating-system-calls.title: Library-level tracing
investigating-system-calls.body: Some problems live above the system call boundary, such as slow DNS resolution in a library or lock contention in user space. ltrace and uprobes trace library function calls, and language-level profilers show managed frames. Combining kernel and user views explains cases where a process issues few system calls yet still spends its time waiting.

investigating-network-and-sockets.title: Listing sockets with ss
investigating-network-and-sockets.body: The ss command lists sockets with state, local and remote addresses, owning process, and queue sizes. For listening sockets, the receive queue shows connections waiting to be accepted and the send queue shows the backlog limit. Many connections in CLOSE_WAIT mean the application is not closing sockets after the peer finished, a common descriptor leak.

investigating-network-and-sockets.title: TCP internals and retransmissions
investigating-network-and-sockets.body: The extended information from ss shows round-trip time, congestion window, retransmissions, and pacing per connection. Counters in nstat or netstat summary output reveal system-wide retransmits, listen queue overflows, and dropped SYNs. Rising retransmissions point at packet loss on the path, while listen overflows mean the application accepts connections too slowly.

investigating-network-and-sockets.title: Capturing packets
investigating-network-and-sockets.body: tcpdump captures traffic matching filters and can save it for analysis in Wireshark. Captures confirm whether requests leave the host, whether responses arrive, and how long each step takes, separating network delay from server delay. Limit captures by host and port and avoid storing sensitive payloads longer than necessary.

investigating-network-and-sockets.title: Name resolution and connection setup
investigating-network-and-sockets.body: Many network issues are not in TCP at all. Slow or failing DNS lookups, exhausted ephemeral ports from many short connections, firewall rules, and connection tracking table limits all produce connection failures or delays. Tools like dig, conntrack, and checking the ephemeral port range help locate these problems before the application layer is suspected.

file-descriptor-exhaustion.title: Recognizing the symptoms
file-descriptor-exhaustion.body: When a process reaches its open file limit, open, socket, accept, and pipe calls fail with EMFILE, often logged as too many open files. Servers stop accepting connections while existing ones continue, so the service looks partly alive. The system-wide limit produces ENFILE instead. Counting entries in /proc/PID/fd and comparing with the limit confirms the diagnosis.

file-descriptor-exhaustion.title: Finding what leaked
file-descriptor-exhaustion.body: lsof or listing /proc/PID/fd shows what each descriptor refers to: files, sockets, pipes, or event objects. Grouping by type and target usually reveals the leak, such as thousands of sockets to one backend or the same log file opened repeatedly. Taking two snapshots minutes apart shows which category grows.

file-descriptor-exhaustion.title: Common leak patterns
file-descriptor-exhaustion.body: Typical causes include error paths that return before closing, connections not returned to a pool, HTTP response bodies never consumed or closed, child processes inheriting descriptors because close-on-exec was not set, and sockets left in CLOSE_WAIT because the application ignores peer shutdown. Language features like try-with-resources, defer, or context managers prevent many of these.

file-descriptor-exhaustion.title: Raising limits is not a fix
file-descriptor-exhaustion.body: Increasing the limit buys time and is appropriate when a service legitimately needs many connections, but it hides real leaks until they exhaust the larger limit or system memory. Monitor open descriptor counts as a metric with alerts, so steady growth is noticed long before it becomes an outage.

profiling-and-flame-graphs.title: Sampling versus instrumentation
profiling-and-flame-graphs.body: A sampling profiler interrupts the program at a fixed rate and records the current stack, giving a statistical picture with low overhead. Instrumentation records every function entry and exit, giving exact counts but distorting timing. Sampling suits production use. Statistical results need enough samples, so short or rare events may require longer collection or event-based triggers.

profiling-and-flame-graphs.title: Reading a flame graph
profiling-and-flame-graphs.body: In a flame graph each box is a function in a stack, the vertical axis is stack depth, and box width is the proportion of samples containing that frame. The x-axis is not time; it is sorted alphabetically to merge identical stacks. Look for wide plateaus at the top, which are functions doing work themselves, and wide frames lower down that lead to them.

profiling-and-flame-graphs.title: On-CPU versus off-CPU profiles
profiling-and-flame-graphs.body: A normal CPU profile shows only time spent executing. If a request is slow because it waits on locks, disks, or network, CPU profiles show little. Off-CPU profiling records stacks when threads block and how long they stay blocked, revealing wait time. Combining both views explains the full latency of a request.

profiling-and-flame-graphs.title: Making stacks readable
profiling-and-flame-graphs.body: Profilers need symbols and frame information to walk stacks. Compiled code built without frame pointers or debug information produces broken stacks, and just-in-time compiled languages need runtime support to map addresses to method names. Getting these prerequisites in place before an incident saves time when profiling matters most.

ebpf-and-bpftrace.title: What eBPF programs are
ebpf-and-bpftrace.body: eBPF lets small programs run inside the kernel when events occur, such as a function entry, a tracepoint, a network packet, or a timer. A verifier checks each program before loading to ensure it terminates and only accesses memory safely, and a just-in-time compiler turns it into native code. Programs store results in maps that user space reads.

ebpf-and-bpftrace.title: Event sources
ebpf-and-bpftrace.body: Kprobes attach to almost any kernel function, uprobes to user-space functions, and tracepoints to stable instrumentation points defined by the kernel. Perf events provide sampling and hardware counters, and USDT probes are markers compiled into applications and runtimes. Tracepoints are preferred when available because kprobe targets can change between kernel versions.

ebpf-and-bpftrace.title: bpftrace for quick questions
ebpf-and-bpftrace.body: bpftrace is a high-level language for one-line and short tracing scripts. A single line can count system calls by process, build a histogram of read sizes, or measure the latency between a function's entry and return. Ready-made tools in the BCC and bpftrace collections cover common questions such as disk latency, new process execution, and TCP retransmits.

ebpf-and-bpftrace.title: Overhead and safety in production
ebpf-and-bpftrace.body: Because aggregation happens in the kernel, eBPF tracing usually adds far less overhead than copying every event to user space. High-frequency probes, such as on every memory allocation, can still slow a system noticeably. Loading programs requires elevated privileges, and the same power used for observability can be misused, so access should be controlled and audited.
